Most speakers treat the ending as the moment to relax, and the audience can feel it. They say that is all, or they thank twenty people by name, and the energy of the room drains away before the applause. I teach executives to plan the last three minutes before they plan anything else. Start with a recap, in one sentence, of the idea that connected everything. Then turn the agreements into commitments: who will have done what, and by when. Then give the room a picture of the future, so that the next meeting already feels real. End with one call to action, not three. And only then say thank you. The last thing the room hears is the first thing it remembers.

If there is one idea to take home from these two days, it is this: the region does not lack capital. It lacks contracts that people trust. So let me turn our agreements into commitments. By the end of March, the ministry will have published its draft concession model. By June, the development bank will have shared a term sheet for a first-loss guarantee. And by the time we meet again in September, at least three funds in this room will have named a project they are studying. We will track all of it on a public scorecard. This time next year, I hope we will be discussing projects under construction, not frameworks on paper. My call to action is simple: follow through on what you said on this stage. And now, with real gratitude, thank you to our sponsors and to all of you.

I will tell you the test I use, and it is not a kind one. Two weeks after the event, I call four people who were in the room and I ask them one question: what are we doing differently? If all four give me a different answer, the closing failed, however good it sounded on the day. The reason is almost always the same. The person closing tried to be fair. They mentioned every panel, thanked every sponsor, and by the end the room had twelve things to remember, which means it had none. A closing address is not a receipt for the week. You are allowed to leave things out. You are supposed to leave things out. The second failure is the date. People will commit to almost anything as long as there is no date attached, and a commitment without a date is just a sentiment in a suit. So I make the closing speaker say the month out loud. Not soon. Not in the coming period. March. Now, one thing people get wrong in the other direction. Do not read out the action list. Fourteen items read aloud is a document, not a speech, and nobody is writing them down. Name three. Put the other eleven in the email that goes out on Monday. And do the debrief inside a week. After ten days people remember what they wish had happened, not what did.
